techniques.name: Factor Analysis
techniques.description: Factor analysis is a statistical technique that identifies latent variables (hidden factors) underlying observed correlations in data. It works by analysing how variables relate to each other, finding a smaller number of unobserved factors that explain patterns among multiple observed variables. Unlike PCA which maximises total variance, factor analysis focuses on shared variance (communalities - the variance variables have in common) whilst separating out unique variance and measurement error. After extracting factors, rotation methods like varimax (which creates uncorrelated factors) or oblimin (allowing correlated factors) help make factors more interpretable by aligning them with distinct groups of variables.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing customer satisfaction surveys to identify key drivers (e.g., 'service quality', 'product value', 'convenience') from dozens of individual questions, helping businesses focus improvement efforts.
Reducing dimensionality of financial indicators to identify underlying economic factors (e.g., 'growth', 'inflation', 'credit risk') for more interpretable risk models.

limitations.description: Assumes linear relationships between variables and multivariate normality of data.
Results can be abstract and require domain expertise to interpret meaningfully.
Sensitive to the choice of number of factors and rotation method, which can significantly affect interpretability.
Requires sufficiently large sample sizes relative to the number of variables for stable results.

Overview and confirmatory and exploratory factor analysis of AI literacy scale
resources.abstract: Comprehensive concepts of AI literacy (AIL) and valid measures are essential for research (e.g., intervention studies) and practice (e.g., personnel selection/development) alike. To date, several scales have been published, sharing standard features but differing in some aspects. We first aim to briefly overview instruments identified from unsystematic literature research in February 2023. We identified four scales and one collection of items. We describe the instruments and compare them. We identified common themes and overlaps in the instruments and developmental procedure. We also found differences regarding scale development procedures and latent dimensions. Following this literature research, we came to the conclusion that the literature on AI literacy measurement was fragmented, and little effort was undertaken to integrate different AI literacy conceptualizations. The second focus of this study is to test the factorial structures of existing AIL measurement instruments and identify latent dimensions of AIL across all instruments. We used robust maximum-likelihood confirmatory factor analysis to test factorial structures in a joint survey of all AIL items in an English-speaking online sample ( N =219). We found general support for all instruments' factorial structures with minor deviations from the original factorial structures for some of the instruments. In a second analysis step, to address the issue of fragmented research on AI literacy conceptualization and measurement, we used principal axis exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation to identify latent dimensions across all items. We found four correlated latent dimensions of AIL, which were mostly interpretable as the abilities to use and interact with AI, to design/program AI (incl. in-depth technical knowledge), to perform complex cognitive operations regarding AI (e.g., ethical considerations), and a common factor for the abilities to detect AI/differentiate between AI and humans and manage persuasive influences of AI (i.e., persuasion literacy). Our findings sort the multitude of AIL instruments and reveal four latent core dimensions of AIL. Thus, they contribute importantly to the conceptual understanding of AIL that has been fragmented so far. • We give an overview of AI literacy measures. • Their factorial structures were mostly confirmed. • PA EFA identified four correlated latent dimensions across all instruments.

techniques.name: Principal Component Analysis
techniques.description: Principal Component Analysis transforms high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional representation by finding the directions (principal components) that capture the maximum variance in the data. Each component is a linear combination of original features, with the first component explaining the most variance, the second component the most remaining variance orthogonal to the first, and so on. This technique reveals underlying patterns in data structure, enables visualisation of complex datasets, and helps identify which combinations of features drive the most variation in the data.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing customer behavior data with dozens of variables (purchase frequency, spending patterns, demographics) to identify the 2-3 main dimensions that explain customer segmentation, revealing whether customers cluster by spending level, product preferences, or shopping frequency.

Reducing dimensionality of image data for facial recognition systems by finding the principal components that capture the most variation in face shapes and expressions, helping understand which facial features contribute most to distinguishing between individuals.

limitations.description: Principal components are abstract linear combinations of original features that often lack clear real-world interpretation or meaning.
Only captures linear relationships between features, missing non-linear patterns and complex interactions in the data.
Results are highly sensitive to feature scaling - features with larger numerical ranges can dominate the principal components.
Information loss is inherent when reducing dimensions, and choosing the optimal number of components requires balancing simplicity with retained variance.

resources.title: Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker? Debiasing Word Embeddings
resources.abstract: The blind application of machine learning runs the risk of amplifying biases present in data. Such a danger is facing us with word embedding, a popular framework to represent text data as vectors which has been used in many machine learning and natural language processing tasks. We show that even word embeddings trained on Google News articles exhibit female/male gender stereotypes to a disturbing extent. This raises concerns because their widespread use, as we describe, often tends to amplify these biases. Geometrically, gender bias is first shown to be captured by a direction in the word embedding. Second, gender neutral words are shown to be linearly separable from gender definition words in the word embedding. Using these properties, we provide a methodology for modifying an embedding to remove gender stereotypes, such as the association between between the words receptionist and female, while maintaining desired associations such as between the words queen and female. We define metrics to quantify both direct and indirect gender biases in embeddings, and develop algorithms to "debias" the embedding. Using crowd-worker evaluation as well as standard benchmarks, we empirically demonstrate that our algorithms significantly reduce gender bias in embeddings while preserving the its useful properties such as the ability to cluster related concepts and to solve analogy tasks. The resulting embeddings can be used in applications without amplifying gender bias.

techniques.name: UMAP
techniques.description: UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a non-linear dimensionality reduction technique that creates 2D or 3D visualisations of high-dimensional data by constructing a mathematical model of the data's underlying manifold structure. Unlike t-SNE, UMAP preserves both local neighbourhood relationships and global topology more effectively, using techniques from topological data analysis and Riemannian geometry. This approach often produces more interpretable cluster layouts while maintaining meaningful distances between clusters, making it particularly valuable for exploratory data analysis and understanding complex dataset structures.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing single-cell RNA sequencing data to visualise how different cell types cluster based on gene expression patterns, revealing developmental trajectories and identifying previously unknown cell subtypes in tissue samples.

Exploring customer segmentation by reducing hundreds of behavioural and demographic features to 2D space, showing how different customer groups relate to each other and identifying transition zones where customers might move between segments.

limitations.description: Hyperparameter choices (n_neighbors, min_dist, metric) significantly influence the embedding structure and can lead to very different interpretations of the same data.
While preserving global structure better than t-SNE, distances in the reduced space still don't directly correspond to distances in the original feature space.
Performance can be sensitive to the choice of distance metric, which may not be obvious for complex or mixed data types.
Like other manifold learning techniques, it assumes the data lies on a lower-dimensional manifold, which may not hold for all datasets.

resources.title: UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction
resources.abstract: UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a novel manifold learning technique for dimension reduction. UMAP is constructed from a theoretical framework based in Riemannian geometry and algebraic topology. The result is a practical scalable algorithm that applies to real world data. The UMAP algorithm is competitive with t-SNE for visualization quality, and arguably preserves more of the global structure with superior run time performance. Furthermore, UMAP has no computational restrictions on embedding dimension, making it viable as a general purpose dimension reduction technique for machine learning.

resources.title: UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection

UMAP has a rigorous mathematical foundation, but is simple to use, with a scikit-learn compatible API. UMAP is among the fastest manifold learning implementations available -significantly faster than most t-SNE implementations.

Dimensionality reduction for visualizing single-cell data using UMAP
resources.abstract: Advances in single-cell technologies have enabled high-resolution dissection of tissue composition. Several tools for dimensionality reduction are available to analyze the large number of parameters generated in single-cell studies. Recently, a nonlinear dimensionality-reduction technique, uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP), was developed for the analysis of any type of high-dimensional data. Here we apply it to biological data, using three well-characterized mass cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. Comparing the performance of UMAP with five other tools, we find that UMAP provides the fastest run times, highest reproducibility and the most meaningful organization of cell clusters. The work highlights the use of UMAP for improved visualization and interpretation of single-cell data.

resources.title: Dimensionality reduction by UMAP to visualize physical and genetic interactions
resources.abstract: Dimensionality reduction is often used to visualize complex expression profiling data. Here, we use the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) method on published transcript profiles of 1484 single gene deletions of Saccharomyces cerevisiae . Proximity in low-dimensional UMAP space identifies groups of genes that correspond to protein complexes and pathways, and finds novel protein interactions, even within well-characterized complexes. This approach is more sensitive than previous methods and should be broadly useful as additional transcriptome datasets become available for other organisms.

techniques.name: GAN-Based Tabular Synthetic Data
techniques.description: Generates synthetic tabular datasets using Generative Adversarial Networks, most commonly through architectures such as CTGAN (Conditional Tabular GAN) and TVAE (Triplet-based Variational Autoencoder). These models learn the joint distribution of mixed-type columns — continuous, discrete, and categorical — by training a generator and discriminator in an adversarial framework, with mode-specific normalisation to handle multimodal continuous distributions and training-by-sampling to address class imbalance. The resulting synthetic tables aim to preserve statistical relationships, correlations, and marginal distributions of the original data whilst containing no real records, supporting privacy-preserving data sharing, model development on sensitive datasets, and augmentation of limited training data.

example_use_cases.description: Generating synthetic patient records from hospital databases using CTGAN to enable multi-institution collaborative research on treatment outcomes without sharing identifiable health data across organisational boundaries.

Augmenting a limited fraud detection training set by generating synthetic fraudulent transaction records that preserve the statistical characteristics of rare fraud patterns, improving model recall on underrepresented fraud types.

Creating balanced synthetic datasets for credit scoring by generating additional records for underrepresented demographic groups, enabling fairness testing across protected characteristics without collecting new sensitive data.

limitations.description: Training instability inherent to GAN architectures (mode collapse, vanishing gradients) can result in synthetic data that fails to capture the full diversity of the original distribution, particularly for rare categories or tail distributions.
Requires substantial computational resources and hyperparameter tuning, with training times scaling poorly for datasets with many columns or complex inter-column dependencies.

Privacy guarantees are not inherent — without additional mechanisms like differential privacy, GAN-generated data may leak information about training records through memorisation or membership inference attacks.
Performance degrades significantly on datasets with high cardinality categorical columns, complex temporal dependencies, or relational structures across multiple tables.

resources.title: Modeling Tabular data using Conditional GAN
resources.abstract: Modeling the probability distribution of rows in tabular data and generating realistic synthetic data is a non-trivial task. Tabular data usually contains a mix of discrete and continuous columns. Continuous columns may have multiple modes whereas discrete columns are sometimes imbalanced making the modeling difficult. Existing statistical and deep neural network models fail to properly model this type of data. We design TGAN, which uses a conditional generative adversarial network to address these challenges. To aid in a fair and thorough comparison, we design a benchmark with 7 simulated and 8 real datasets and several Bayesian network baselines. TGAN outperforms Bayesian methods on most of the real datasets whereas other deep learning methods could not.

A Review of Tabular Data Synthesis Using GANs on an IDS Dataset
resources.abstract: Recent technological innovations along with the vast amount of available data worldwide have led to the rise of cyberattacks against network systems. Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) play a crucial role as a defense mechanism in networks against adversarial attackers. Machine Learning methods provide various cybersecurity tools. However, these methods require plenty of data to be trained efficiently, which may be hard to collect or to use due to privacy reasons. One of the most notable Machine Learning tools is the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), and it has great potential for tabular data synthesis. In this work, we start by briefly presenting the most popular GAN architectures, VanillaGAN, WGAN, and WGAN-GP. Focusing on tabular data generation, CTGAN, CopulaGAN, and TableGAN models are used for the creation of synthetic IDS data. Specifically, the models are trained and evaluated on an NSL-KDD dataset, considering the limitations and requirements that this procedure needs. Finally, based on certain quantitative and qualitative methods, we argue and evaluate the most prominent GANs for tabular network data synthesis.

techniques.name: Sequential CART Synthesis
techniques.description: Sequential CART synthesis creates an artificial copy of a confidential microdata set (records about individual people or organisations) that can be released in place of the real data, in the form used by the synthpop package for R. Variables are synthesised one at a time in a chosen order: the first is generated by sampling with replacement from its observed values, and for each later variable a classification or regression tree (CART) is fitted on the real data to predict it from the variables earlier in the order. Each synthetic record is passed down that tree using its already-synthesised values, and the new value is copied from a randomly chosen real record in the leaf it reaches, so the joint distribution of the data is rebuilt as a chain of conditional distributions. Disclosure risk is limited by setting a minimum leaf size, smoothing synthesised continuous values and removing synthetic records that reproduce unique real ones, and several synthetic copies can be released so that analysts can allow for the extra uncertainty that synthesis adds.

example_use_cases.description: A national longitudinal study that links census returns to administrative records such as births, deaths and cancer registrations for a sample of the population cannot let approved researchers take the data off site. Its support team runs CART synthesis to produce a bespoke synthetic extract for each project, so researchers can explore the data and write and test their analysis code at their own institution before the final model is run on the real data in the secure setting.

A hospital trust wants a university team to develop a readmission model without receiving patient records. It releases a CART-synthesised copy of the admissions table with a minimum leaf size of ten and kernel smoothing of continuous values, removes any synthetic record that matches a unique real patient on age, sex and postcode district, and runs a disclosure-risk assessment before release.

A national statistics office publishes a synthetic teaching file of its labour force survey for university courses, generated by sequential CART synthesis with the variable order and minimum leaf sizes chosen with subject experts, and labels every record as synthetic so that no reader mistakes a row for a real respondent.

limitations.description: It gives no formal privacy guarantee. No synthetic record is a real person, but trees can reproduce rare combinations and extreme values, and an intruder who knows that a real record holds the largest value of a variable can bound it from the synthetic maximum. Risk must be measured for each release and reduced with larger leaves, smoothing and removal of unique matches, each of which costs analytical value.

Relationships the trees miss disappear from the synthetic data. A tree grown from few records may never split on a variable that matters, so the synthetic data show no association where the real data have one; in the method's original evaluation a regression coefficient for sex was attenuated to zero in this way. Small subgroups and weak effects are the most exposed.

Results depend on the order in which variables are synthesised and on which earlier variables predict each later one. A careless order can produce impossible combinations, such as a detailed category that contradicts the summary variable derived from it, so detailed variables should be synthesised before derived ones and the output checked for inconsistencies.

Synthetic data cannot reproduce every analysis of the real data. Analyses the synthesiser did not plan for may give different answers, so a release should state which analyses it supports, and users should confirm key findings on the real data, for example through a verification service or secure access.

resources.title: synthpop: Bespoke Creation of Synthetic Data in R
resources.abstract: In many contexts, confidentiality constraints severely restrict access to unique and valuable microdata. Synthetic data which mimic the original observed data and preserve the relationships between variables but do not contain any disclosive records are one possible solution to this problem. The synthpop package for R, introduced in this paper, provides routines to generate synthetic versions of original data sets. We describe the methodology and its consequences for the data characteristics. We illustrate the package features using a survey data example.

resources.title: synthpop: Generating Synthetic Versions of Sensitive Microdata for Statistical Disclosure Control
resources.abstract: A tool for producing synthetic versions of microdata containing confidential information so that they are safe to be released to users for exploratory analysis. The key objective of generating synthetic data is to replace sensitive original values with synthetic ones causing minimal distortion of the statistical information contained in the data set. Variables, which can be categorical or continuous, are synthesised one-by-one using sequential modelling. Replacements are generated by drawing from conditional distributions fitted to the original data using parametric or classification and regression trees models. Data are synthesised via the function syn() which can be largely automated, if default settings are used, or with methods defined by the user. Optional parameters can be used to influence the disclosure risk and the analytical quality of the synthesised data. For a description of the implemented method see Nowok, Raab and Dibben (2016) <doi:10.18637/jss.v074.i11>. Functions to assess identity and attribute disclosure for the original and for the synthetic data are included in the package, and their use is illustrated in a vignette on disclosure (Practical Privacy Metrics for Synthetic Data).

resources.title: Using CART to Generate Partially Synthetic Public Use Microdata
resources.abstract: To limit disclosure risks, one approach is to release partially synthetic public use microdata sets. These comprise the units originally surveyed, but some collected values, for example sensitive values at high risk of disclosure or values of key identifiers, are replaced with multiple imputations. This article presents and evaluates the use of classification and regression trees to generate partially synthetic data. Two potential applications of CART are studied via simulation: (i) generate synthetic data for sensitive variables; and, (ii) generate synthetic data for variables that are key identifiers.

resources.abstract: Synthetic data methods were designed to address the conflicting demands placed on data holders to unlock the research and policy potential of microdata while at the same time preserving the confidentiality of individuals.Recently, these methods have become more widely recognized in the UK and the provision of bespoke synthetic data has been approved to expand the use of one of the UK Longitudinal Studies.The process of producing useful synthetic data involves, however, a substantial investment of research time, as it always requires some customising for the characteristics of an individual data set.At the same time, a substantial part of it can be automated and this is essential when the process has to be conducted rapidly and on a regular basis.This paper describes the application of synthetic data to the UK Longitudinal Studies, details implementation process for the Scottish Longitudinal Study and presents methods used in an R package synthpop that has been developed to facilitate production of non-disclosive entirely synthetic data.A reproducible example using open data is given to illustrate the synthesising procedure and to provide insights into quality of synthetic data generated using different automated approaches.

techniques.name: Algorithm Review Boards
techniques.description: An algorithm review board is a standing, multidisciplinary body inside an organisation that examines proposed AI systems or AI research projects at set points and decides whether, and on what conditions, they may proceed. The literature also calls these bodies AI ethics boards or AI review boards. They differ from an Institutional Review Board (IRB), which protects the human subjects of research, because they also weigh harms to the people a system will affect and to society. A risk-based triage decides which projects need full review; the project team then submits a written account of the system's purpose, data, foreseeable harms and planned mitigations, and members drawn from technical, legal, ethical and domain backgrounds, sometimes with people from affected communities, question the team and iterate on that account with them. The board approves, approves with conditions such as a monitoring plan or a re-review date, or rejects, and the output is a dated decision record with its reasons and conditions that later reviews and audits can check against what was built.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group's algorithm review board examines a sepsis early-warning model before a ward pilot. It approves the pilot on condition of a monitoring plan for alert rates and missed cases, names who may switch the model off, and sets a re-review once six months of local performance data are in, before any wider roll-out.

A bank's board reviews a proposed credit-limit model before launch. It asks the team for its disparate-impact analysis by protected group and for evidence that applicants can contest a decision, and withholds approval until both are supplied, so the decision to deploy rests with a body outside the development team.

A university AI research programme releases grant funding only after each project has passed an ethics and society review, in which researchers state the risks their work poses to society and to particular groups, commit to mitigations, and revise them with an interdisciplinary faculty panel.

A government department publishes the board's decision record for a benefits-triage tool, giving the reasons for approval, the conditions attached and the re-review date, so that its oversight committee and the public can see what was examined, by whom and when, and check later that the conditions were met.

limitations.description: Review adds time and cost to every project that goes through it, and organisations under commercial pressure may route work around the board or narrow its remit, so the board's coverage, not just its existence, needs to be shown.

Its judgements are only as good as its membership. A board without the relevant technical, domain or community expertise will miss harms that fall outside what its members know, and a board drawn mainly from inside the team's own reporting line is open to group-think.

Independence is hard to keep inside an organisation. Practitioners report tension between profit and the cost of responsible-AI review, and a board can come under pressure to approve projects that leadership has already committed to, which weakens it most where review matters most.

Without authority to stop or delay a project, and a way to check that its conditions are met, a board's recommendations can be ignored. Evidence from a board is strong only when its decision record shows what it could block and what happened to its conditions.

There is no agreed measure of whether a board works, and review can become box-ticking. A record that a project was reviewed shows that a process ran, not that the review was substantive or that its concerns were addressed.

resources.title: How to design an AI ethics board
resources.abstract: The development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) systems poses significant risks to society. To reduce these risks to an acceptable level, AI companies need an effective risk management process and sound risk governance. In this paper, we explore a particular way in which AI companies can improve their risk governance: by setting up an AI ethics board. We identify five key design choices: (1) What responsibilities should the board have? (2) What should its legal structure be? (3) Who should sit on the board? (4) How should it make decisions? (5) And what resources does it need? We break each of these questions down into more specific sub-questions, list options, and discuss how different design choices affect the board’s ability to reduce societal risks from AI. Several failures have shown that designing an AI ethics board can be challenging. This paper provides a toolbox that can help AI companies to overcome these challenges.

resources.title: Designing Artificial Intelligence Review Boards: Creating Risk Metrics for Review of AI
resources.abstract: Discussions of the need for a review committee dedicated to ethical oversight of artificial intelligence (AI) research have not yet advanced to organization design discussions. What are the essential components for an AI research review board? Based upon precedent for composition and conduct of high-technology review boards, one essential component is a risk-adjusted review mechanism that assists review boards in the categorization of research needing review. In this paper, risk assessment tools are developed based upon lessons learned from other review boards, such as Institutional Biosafety Committees.

resources.title: Ethics and society review: Ethics reflection as a precondition to research funding
resources.abstract: Researchers in areas as diverse as computer science and political science must increasingly navigate the possible risks of their research to society. However, the history of medical experiments on vulnerable individuals influenced many research ethics reviews to focus exclusively on risks to human subjects rather than risks to human society. We describe an Ethics and Society Review board (ESR), which fills this moral gap by facilitating ethical and societal reflection as a requirement to access grant funding: Researchers cannot receive grant funding from participating programs until the researchers complete the ESR process for their proposal. Researchers author an initial statement describing their proposed research’s risks to society, subgroups within society, and globally and commit to mitigation strategies for these risks. An interdisciplinary faculty panel iterates with the researchers to refine these risks and mitigation strategies. We describe a mixed-method evaluation of the ESR over 1 y, in partnership with an artificial intelligence grant program run by Stanford HAI. Surveys and interviews of researchers who interacted with the ESR found 100% (95% CI: 87 to 100%) were willing to continue submitting future projects to the ESR, and 58% (95% CI: 37 to 77%) felt that it had influenced the design of their research project. The ESR panel most commonly identified issues of harms to minority groups, inclusion of diverse stakeholders in the research plan, dual use, and representation in datasets. These principles, paired with possible mitigation strategies, offer scaffolding for future research designs.

resources.title: ESR Process & Toolkit — Stanford Ethics & Society Review
resources.abstract: The Ethics and Society Review is improving ethical reflection in research by bringing together a panel of ethics experts to help researchers identify and mitigate negative ethical or societal aspects of their research and elevate the positive.

resources.title: Investigating Algorithm Review Boards for Organizational Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance
resources.abstract: Organizations are increasingly developing and utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) tools. Responsible AI (RAI) governance approaches including algorithm review board (ARBs) have emerged as important mechanisms to address potential AI risks and harms. We interviewed 17 technical contributors at a variety of organizations about their experiences with internal RAI governance. We summarized the first detailed findings on ARBs in practice, including their membership, scope, and measures of success. We confirmed known ARBs in finance sectors and revealed extensive use of ARBs in health sectors. Our findings suggest that Institutional Review Boards alone are insufficient for algorithm governance and that ARBs are used in tandem with other RAI approaches. Integration with existing processes and leadership buy-in were considered critical to the success of internal RAI governance. Financial tensions between profit and the cost of RAI were a major concern for many participants. Future work should explore measurements of success for ARBs and expand analysis of ARBs to other industries leading in AI implementation.

resources.title: A framework for the oversight and local deployment of safe and high-quality prediction models
resources.abstract: Artificial intelligence/machine learning models are being rapidly developed and used in clinical practice. However, many models are deployed without a clear understanding of clinical or operational impact and frequently lack monitoring plans that can detect potential safety signals. There is a lack of consensus in establishing governance to deploy, pilot, and monitor algorithms within operational healthcare delivery workflows. Here, we describe a governance framework that combines current regulatory best practices and lifecycle management of predictive models being used for clinical care. Since January 2021, we have successfully added models to our governance portfolio and are currently managing 52 models.

The conditions the review board attached to the credit-limit model's approval, including a disparate-impact analysis by protected group and a re-review date, were met before and after launch

The diagnostic AI system's development and deployment decisions are traceable to dated board decision records that state the risks assessed, the reasons for approval and the conditions attached
The review board's decision record for the risk assessment tool, with its reasons and conditions, is available to the oversight body and the public

techniques.name: Datasheets for Datasets
techniques.description: Datasheets for datasets establish comprehensive documentation standards for datasets, systematically recording creation methodology, data composition, collection procedures, preprocessing transformations, intended applications, potential biases, privacy considerations, and maintenance protocols. These structured documents enhance dataset transparency by providing essential context for appropriate usage, enabling informed decisions about dataset suitability for specific tasks, supporting bias detection and mitigation efforts, ensuring compliance with data protection regulations, and promoting responsible data stewardship throughout the entire data lifecycle from collection to disposal.

example_use_cases.description: Documenting a medical imaging dataset with detailed information about patient privacy protections, anonymisation procedures, and data sharing constraints to ensure sensitive health information is handled appropriately and regulatory compliance is maintained.

Creating comprehensive datasheets for recruitment datasets that document demographic representation across different job categories, helping developers identify potential bias in training data and develop more equitable hiring algorithms.

Establishing transparent documentation for financial transaction datasets that clearly describes data collection methodology, preprocessing steps, and intended use cases, enabling researchers to make informed decisions about dataset appropriateness for their specific applications.

Documenting a safety-critical autonomous vehicle perception dataset with records of sensor calibration procedures, environmental conditions during collection, edge-case scenario coverage, and known distributional gaps, enabling safety engineers to assess whether training data adequately represents the operating conditions required for safe deployment and to support regulatory type-approval submissions.

Information may become outdated as datasets undergo preprocessing, cleaning, or augmentation, requiring ongoing maintenance to ensure documentation accuracy throughout the data lifecycle.
Absence of standardised templates and enforcement mechanisms leads to inconsistent documentation quality and completeness across different organisations and research communities.
Dataset creators may intentionally omit sensitive information about collection methods, participant consent, or potential biases to avoid legal liability or competitive disadvantage.
Limited adoption and awareness means many existing datasets lack proper documentation, creating gaps in the historical record and making legacy dataset assessment difficult.

resources.title: Datasheets for Datasets
resources.abstract: The machine learning community currently has no standardized process for documenting datasets, which can lead to severe consequences in high-stakes domains. To address this gap, we propose datasheets for datasets. In the electronics industry, every component, no matter how simple or complex, is accompanied with a datasheet that describes its operating characteristics, test results, recommended uses, and other information. By analogy, we propose that every dataset be accompanied with a datasheet that documents its motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and so on. Datasheets for datasets will facilitate better communication between dataset creators and dataset consumers, and encourage the machine learning community to prioritize transparency and accountability.

resources.title: Understanding Machine Learning Practitioners' Data Documentation Perceptions, Needs, Challenges, and Desiderata
resources.abstract: Data is central to the development and evaluation of machine learning (ML) models. However, the use of problematic or inappropriate datasets can result in harms when the resulting models are deployed. To encourage responsible AI practice through more deliberate reflection on datasets and transparency around the processes by which they are created, researchers and practitioners have begun to advocate for increased data documentation and have proposed several data documentation frameworks. However, there is little research on whether these data documentation frameworks meet the needs of ML practitioners, who both create and consume datasets. To address this gap, we set out to understand ML practitioners' data documentation perceptions, needs, challenges, and desiderata, with the goal of deriving design requirements that can inform future data documentation frameworks. We conducted a series of semi-structured interviews with 14 ML practitioners at a single large, international technology company. We had them answer a list of questions taken from datasheets for datasets (Gebru, 2021). Our findings show that current approaches to data documentation are largely ad hoc and myopic in nature. Participants expressed needs for data documentation frameworks to be adaptable to their contexts, integrated into their existing tools and workflows, and automated wherever possible. Despite the fact that data documentation frameworks are often motivated from the perspective of responsible AI, participants did not make the connection between the questions that they were asked to answer and their responsible AI implications. In addition, participants often had difficulties prioritizing the needs of dataset consumers and providing information that someone unfamiliar with their datasets might need to know. Based on these findings, we derive seven design requirements for future data documentation frameworks.

resources.title: Datasheets for Datasets help ML Engineers Notice and Understand Ethical Issues in Training Data
resources.abstract: The social computing community has demonstrated interest in the ethical issues sometimes produced by machine learning (ML) models, like violations of privacy, fairness, and accountability. This paper discovers what kinds of ethical considerations machine learning engineers recognize, how they build understanding, and what decisions they make when working with a real-world dataset. In particular, it illustrates ways in which Datasheets for Datasets, an accountability intervention designed to help engineers explore unfamiliar training data, scaffolds the process of issue discovery, understanding, and ethical decision-making. Participants were asked to review an intentionally ethically problematic dataset and asked to think aloud as they used it to solve a given ML problem. Out of 23 participants, 11 were given a Datasheet they could use while completing the task. Participants were ethically sensitive enough to identify concerns in the dataset; participants who had a Datasheet did open and refer to it; and those with Datasheets mentioned ethical issues during the think-aloud earlier and more often than than those without. The think-aloud protocol offered a grounded description of how participants recognized, understood, and made a decision about ethical problems in an unfamiliar dataset. The method used in this study can test other interventions that claim to encourage recognition, promote understanding, and support decision-making among technologists.

techniques.name: Fairness GAN
techniques.description: A data generation technique that employs Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to create fair synthetic datasets by learning to generate data representations that preserve utility whilst obfuscating protected attributes. Unlike traditional GANs, Fairness GANs incorporate fairness constraints into the training objective, ensuring that the generated data maintains statistical parity across demographic groups. The technique can be used for data augmentation to balance underrepresented groups or to create privacy-preserving synthetic datasets that remove demographic bias from training data.

example_use_cases.description: Generating balanced synthetic datasets for medical research by creating additional samples from underrepresented demographic groups, ensuring equal representation across ethnicity and gender whilst maintaining the statistical properties needed for robust model training.

limitations.description: GAN training is notoriously difficult to stabilise, with potential for mode collapse or failure to converge, especially when additional fairness constraints are imposed.
Ensuring fairness in generated data may come at the cost of data utility, potentially reducing the quality or realism of synthetic samples.
Requires large datasets to train both generator and discriminator networks effectively, limiting applicability in data-scarce domains.
Evaluation complexity is high, as it requires assessing both the quality of generated data and the preservation of fairness properties across demographic groups.
May inadvertently introduce new biases if the fairness constraints are not properly specified or if the training data itself contains subtle biases.

resources.title: TabFairGAN
Fairness GAN
resources.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Fairness GAN, an approach for generating a dataset that is plausibly similar to a given multimedia dataset, but is more fair with respect to protected attributes in allocative decision making. We propose a novel auxiliary classifier GAN that strives for demographic parity or equality of opportunity and show empirical results on several datasets, including the CelebFaces Attributes (CelebA) dataset, the Quick, Draw!\ dataset, and a dataset of soccer player images and the offenses they were called for. The proposed formulation is well-suited to absorbing unlabeled data; we leverage this to augment the soccer dataset with the much larger CelebA dataset. The methodology tends to improve demographic parity and equality of opportunity while generating plausible images.

resources.title: FairGAN: Fairness-aware Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Fairness-aware learning is increasingly important in data mining. Discrimination prevention aims to prevent discrimination in the training data before it is used to conduct predictive analysis. In this paper, we focus on fair data generation that ensures the generated data is discrimination free. Inspired by generative adversarial networks (GAN), we present fairness-aware generative adversarial networks, called FairGAN, which are able to learn a generator producing fair data and also preserving good data utility. Compared with the naive fair data generation models, FairGAN further ensures the classifiers which are trained on generated data can achieve fair classification on real data. Experiments on a real dataset show the effectiveness of FairGAN.

resources.title: Bt-GAN: Generating Fair Synthetic Healthdata via Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Synthetic data generation offers a promising solution to enhance the usefulness of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) by generating realistic de-identified data. However, the existing literature primarily focuses on the quality of synthetic health data, neglecting the crucial aspect of fairness in downstream predictions. Consequently, models trained on synthetic EHR have faced criticism for producing biased outcomes in target tasks. These biases can arise from either spurious correlations between features or the failure of models to accurately represent sub-groups. To address these concerns, we present Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks (Bt-GAN), a GAN-based synthetic data generator specifically designed for the healthcare domain. In order to tackle spurious correlations (i), we propose an information-constrained Data Generation Process (DGP) that enables the generator to learn a fair deterministic transformation based on a well-defined notion of algorithmic fairness. To overcome the challenge of capturing exact sub-group representations (ii), we incentivize the generator to preserve sub-group densities through score-based weighted sampling. This approach compels the generator to learn from underrepresented regions of the data manifold. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-III) database. Our results demonstrate that Bt-GAN achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while significantly improving fairness and minimizing bias amplification. Furthermore, we perform an in-depth explainability analysis to provide additional evidence supporting the validity of our study. In conclusion, our research introduces a novel and professional approach to addressing the limitations of synthetic data generation in the healthcare domain. By incorporating fairness considerations and leveraging advanced techniques such as GANs, we pave the way for more reliable and unbiased predictions in healthcare applications.

resources.title: FairFinGAN: Fairness-Aware Synthetic Financial Data Generation
resources.abstract: Financial datasets often suffer from bias that can lead to unfair decision-making in automated systems. In this work, we propose FairFinGAN, a WGAN-based framework designed to generate synthetic financial data while mitigating bias with respect to the protected attribute. Our approach incorporates fairness constraints directly into the training process through a classifier, ensuring that the synthetic data is both fair and preserves utility for downstream predictive tasks. We evaluate our proposed model on five real-world financial datasets and compare it with existing GAN-based data generation methods. Experimental results show that our approach achieves superior fairness metrics without significant loss in data utility, demonstrating its potential as a tool for bias-aware data generation in financial applications.

techniques.name: Cross-Modal Consistency Scoring
techniques.description: Cross-modal consistency scoring checks whether content in one modality matches content in another, such as an image and its caption, a generated image and the prompt that produced it, or an audio clip and its description. It uses a contrastively trained model, one that has learned from large collections of paired examples to turn each item into an embedding (a numerical vector describing its content) and to place matching pairs close together: CLIP, trained on image-caption pairs, for images and text, or CLAP, its audio-and-text counterpart, for audio and text. The score for a pair is the cosine similarity of its two embeddings; in the standard image form, CLIPScore, negative similarities are set to zero and the result is rescaled, and no human-written reference is needed. A practitioner scores every pair in an evaluation set or in production, sets a threshold against a sample of human judgements, and then compares average scores between systems or sends pairs below the threshold for review. The score shows whether two items are about the same things, not whether every detail of a description is correct.

example_use_cases.description: A public library deploying an automatic alt-text generator for its digitised photograph collection scores every generated description against its image and routes those below a threshold, set on a sample rated by staff, to a cataloguer, so that descriptions of the wrong subject are caught before visitors using screen readers meet them; names, dates and places in the descriptions are checked separately.

A design-software company deciding whether to ship a new version of its text-to-image model generates images for the same few thousand varied prompts with fixed random seeds, compares the average image-prompt scores of the old and new versions, and checks the comparison against human ratings on a subset before release.

A team assembling an image-caption training set from web data drops pairs whose image-text similarity falls below a threshold, as the builders of LAION-5B did, and audits a sample of the discarded pairs by subject and demographic group before accepting the filter, because such filters remove some groups' images at higher rates.

A broadcaster's archive team generating text descriptions for an untagged sound-effects library scores each description against its clip with an audio-text model, uses the scores only to order clips for human listening checks rather than to accept descriptions automatically, and records the agreement between scores and listeners' judgements.

limitations.description: Contrastively trained image-text models largely ignore word order, relations between objects and which attribute belongs to which object, so a description that names the right things in the wrong relationship can score almost as well as a correct one. The score checks that the right content is mentioned, not that the description of how it fits together is right.

It cannot check what is not visible or audible. Names, places, events and other context in a news photograph or an archive recording are outside what the encoder can match, and the original authors found the image score weaker than reference-based metrics on news captions, so it should not be the only check where such facts matter.

Scores inherit the encoder's training data, which is mostly web alt-text, and its biases. An audit of CLIP-based filtering found that data associated with LGBTQ+ people, older women and younger men was excluded at higher rates, so a single threshold can be stricter for some subjects than others and needs checking by group.

Scores have no absolute meaning: they depend on the encoder checkpoint and on the tool's scaling (the original CLIPScore multiplies the cosine similarity by 2.5, torchmetrics by 100), so values are not comparable across checkpoints or tools. The default CLIP text encoder also reads at most 77 tokens, so longer descriptions are judged on their opening only. Thresholds must be set and reported for the specific model and settings used.

The audio form is weaker still: CLAP-based scores have been found to correlate only weakly with human ratings of how well audio matches its text, so for audio the score is a coarse screen to prioritise human checks rather than evidence of consistency on its own.

resources.title: CLIPScore: A Reference-free Evaluation Metric for Image Captioning
resources.abstract: Image captioning has conventionally relied on reference-based automatic evaluations, where machine captions are compared against captions written by humans.This is in contrast to the reference-free manner in which humans assess caption quality.In this paper, we report the surprising empirical finding that CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), a cross-modal model pretrained on 400M im-age+caption pairs from the web, can be used for robust automatic evaluation of image captioning without the need for references.Experiments spanning several corpora demonstrate that our new reference-free metric, CLIPScore, achieves the highest correlation with human judgements, outperforming existing reference-based metrics like CIDEr and SPICE.Information gain experiments demonstrate that CLIPScore, with its tight focus on image-text compatibility, is complementary to existing reference-based metrics that emphasize text-text similarities.Thus, we also present a reference-augmented version, RefCLIPScore, which achieves even higher correlation.Beyond literal description tasks, several case studies reveal domains where CLIPScore performs well (clip-art images, alt-text rating), but also where it is relatively weaker in comparison to reference-based metrics, e.g., news captions that require richer contextual knowledge.

Who's in and who's out? A case study of multimodal CLIP-filtering in DataComp
resources.abstract: As training datasets become increasingly drawn from unstructured, uncontrolled environments such as the web, researchers and industry practitioners have increasingly relied upon data filtering techniques to “filter out the noise” of web-scraped data. While datasets have been widely shown to reflect the biases and values of their creators, in this paper we contribute to an emerging body of research that assesses the filters used to create these datasets. We show that image-text data filtering also has biases and is value-laden, encoding specific notions of what is counted as “high-quality” data. In our work, we audit a standard approach of image-text CLIP-filtering on the academic benchmark DataComp’s CommonPool by analyzing discrepancies of filtering through various annotation techniques across multiple modalities of image, text, and website source. We find that data relating to several imputed demographic groups — such as LGBTQ+ people, older women, and younger men — are associated with higher rates of exclusion. We also find prevalence of Western bias, where the CLIP filter is more likely to include data related to Western countries compared to that of non-Western countries. Moreover, we demonstrate cases of exclusion amplification: not only are certain marginalized groups already underrepresented in the unfiltered data, but CLIP-filtering excludes data from these groups at higher rates. The data-filtering step in the machine learning pipeline can therefore exacerbate representation disparities already present in the data-gathering step, especially when existing filters are designed to optimize a specifically-chosen downstream performance metric like zero-shot image classification accuracy. Finally, we show that the NSFW filter fails to remove sexually-explicit content from CommonPool, and that CLIP-filtering includes several categories of copyrighted content at high rates. Our conclusions point to a need for fundamental changes in dataset creation and filtering practices. Content warning: This paper discusses societal stereotypes and sexually-explicit material that may be disturbing, distressing, and/or offensive to the reader.

techniques.name: STRIDE-AI Threat Modelling
techniques.description: STRIDE-AI is a threat-modelling method for machine-learning (ML) systems, proposed by Mauri and Damiani (2021, extended 2022), that lists, before any testing, the ways an attacker could compromise each asset of an ML pipeline and how serious each would be. It adapts Microsoft's STRIDE scheme, in which each of six threat types (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege) breaks one security property (authenticity, integrity, non-repudiation, confidentiality, availability and authorisation), and gives each property an ML-specific definition: confidentiality, for example, means that querying a model reveals nothing beyond its inputs and outputs. The analyst surveys the assets produced across the ML life cycle, such as raw, labelled and validation data, hyperparameters, trained and deployed models and the model architecture, and with each asset's owners runs a failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA, a structured review of how a component could fail and with what effect), answering set questions about how the asset could fail, be misused or be abused. Each failure mode is mapped to the properties it would break and so to STRIDE threats, using the method's published tables of asset types, properties and known attacks; the analyst then works with developers to draw threat trees showing the conditions under which each threat could be realised, and rates each threat's priority (the worked example uses DREAD, which scores five factors from 1 to 10). The output is a threat model, a table of assets, threatened properties, threats and priorities with their threat trees: the method attacks and measures nothing, and choosing and testing controls for the threats it finds is left to other techniques.

example_use_cases.description: The security architect for a solar-farm operator's fault-prediction service, which trains on sensor readings streamed from plant data loggers to an external ML platform, maps each asset to its threatened properties. The threat trees show that the loggers' signatures stop injected readings but not label flipping, because labels are added later on the operator's own platform, so that threat is ranked and passed to the platform team.

Before buying a third-party chest X-ray triage model, a hospital's information-security team runs STRIDE-AI over the vendor's pipeline documentation: training data, the supplied model file, the inference service and the results sent to radiologists. Threats such as tampering with the model file and disclosure of training images through model outputs set the scope of the security tests and contract terms the hospital asks the vendor to meet.

A bank's model-security lead repeats the analysis when a card-fraud model moves from monthly retraining to online learning on live transactions. The transaction stream becomes a training-data asset that anyone making transactions can influence, so tampering with it to drift the model is added as a threat, rated and entered in the bank's risk register.

limitations.description: A finished threat model is not evidence that no other threats exist. Its coverage depends on the asset survey and on what the analysts know; the authors state that ML vulnerabilities cannot be fully enumerated in one pass and that failure modes must be updated as the system and known attacks change, and a 2006 Microsoft account of STRIDE notes there is no well-established way to measure a threat model's quality. Claims should state what was in scope and when the analysis was last revised.

STRIDE-AI identifies and ranks threats but does not choose or test controls. Both papers' abstracts say it guides control selection, but neither gives a procedure: the 2021 paper puts control selection outside its scope and the 2022 paper leaves it to future work, noting that no security control framework designed for ML was available. A claim that the threats are mitigated needs separate evidence, such as attack tests against each control and a control catalogue taken from another source.

Priorities are expert judgements. The worked example uses DREAD scores, which the authors note can give inconsistent results between raters and are no longer recommended as the only basis for ranking. Two teams may rank the same threats differently, so claims that rest on the ranking are stronger when several people score independently or a published severity scale such as a bug bar is used.

The mapping from failure modes to properties and threats is done by hand for every asset, and needs asset owners, developers and a security analyst together. Later work describes it as lacking automation, which limits how far it scales to large pipelines; each significant change, such as moving a model to online learning, means repeating part of the analysis.

The published catalogue of assets, failure modes and known attacks was built in 2021-22 around the life cycle of a conventionally trained model, from requirements to maintenance. It does not list assets specific to language-model applications and agents, such as system prompts, retrieval corpora or connected tools, so analysts of those systems must add the assets and their threats themselves, without guidance from the method.

techniques.name: Attacker-Model Re-identification Risk Measurement
techniques.description: Attacker-model re-identification risk measurement estimates, for a table of real records about people that is about to be released or shared, the probability that an attacker who links it with other information could correctly match a record to the person it describes. This record follows the attacker models of El Emam and Dankar (prosecutor and journalist) and of Dankar and El Emam (marketer), as implemented in the ARX tool: the assessor lists the quasi-identifiers (columns such as age, sex, postcode and admission date that an attacker could know or find), groups the records that share the same values on them, and names the attacker being guarded against. For a prosecutor, who knows the target is in the table, a record's risk is one over the size of its group in the table; for a journalist, who does not know this and links to a register of the wider population, it is one over the size of the matching group in that population, estimated with a statistical model when the population counts are not known; for a marketer, who tries to match as many records as possible, the measure is the expected share of records matched correctly. The assessor reports the highest record risk, the average risk and the share of records above a threshold set for the release, which decides whether the table can go out as it is or needs more generalisation or suppression first. It measures how easily records can be matched to people under the stated assumptions, unlike k-anonymity, which transforms the data, and it does not measure what can be learned about someone from values their whole group shares.

example_use_cases.description: A health insurer releasing claims data for a public prediction competition assumes an attacker who knows a neighbour's age, sex and a few of their claims, and measures each record's risk as one over the size of its group among all the insurer's members. It generalises ages and procedure codes until the measured probability of re-identification is below the 0.05 threshold agreed for the release, then checks the result with simulated matching attacks.

A pharmaceutical company sharing participant-level data from a completed trial with external researchers measures risk against the wider population, not the trial sample, because the participants are a small sample of everyone with the condition. It estimates how many records are unique in that population with ARX's uniqueness models and records the quasi-identifiers, attacker model, estimator and threshold in the data-sharing agreement for the researchers' data access committee to review.

A city transport authority planning to give a commuting dataset of home district, work district, age band and usual travel times to a contractor training a demand-forecasting model runs the assessment, finds a large share of records unique on home and work district together, merges small districts before sharing, and re-runs the assessment to confirm that the share of records above its threshold has fallen below the agreed limit.

limitations.description: The numbers are only as good as the list of quasi-identifiers and the attacker model behind them. A column left off the list, or an attacker who knows more (several of a person's hospital visits rather than one), can make records far easier to match than the assessment reports, and the assessor has to guess what other data an attacker holds. Repeating the assessment for stronger attackers, as some releases do with simulated matching, shows how sensitive the result is to these guesses.

It measures the chance of finding which record is a person's, not what can be learned about them. If all 20 records in a group share the same diagnosis, each has a measured risk of 1 in 20, yet anyone known to belong to the group has their diagnosis disclosed. Checks on the sensitive values, such as l-diversity, are needed alongside it when the release contains sensitive columns.

The journalist measure needs to know how common each record's values are in the wider population, which is rarely known and is estimated from the sample with statistical models; an evaluation of four estimators of population uniqueness on six clinical datasets found none accurate in all conditions. A small sample does not make re-identification unlikely in itself: one study estimated that 15 demographic attributes would let 99.98 per cent of Americans be correctly re-identified in any dataset.

There is no universal threshold, and the measure chosen changes the answer. For the same records the prosecutor measure is always at least as high as the journalist measure, so applying it to a release that is a small sample of a population over-protects and strips detail the data's users need; El Emam and Dankar found this effect strongest at small sampling fractions. The threshold, and which measure it applies to, must be justified for each release.

It measures one table as released, at one time. An attacker can combine several releases of the same data, or successive versions of a table that is updated, and longitudinal data, where each person has many events, need the attacker's knowledge of several events to be modelled explicitly. The basic measures do neither, so each additional or updated release needs its own assessment that takes the earlier ones into account.

techniques.name: k-Anonymity
techniques.description: k-Anonymity is a property that a table of real records about people can be made to satisfy before it is released or shared, in which every record shares its values on the quasi-identifiers with at least k-1 other records, so anyone linking the table to another source on those columns always matches a group of at least k records, which is k people only when each person has one record. Quasi-identifiers are columns that are not names or ID numbers but could be found elsewhere and combined to single a person out, such as date of birth, sex and postcode, and because the data holder chooses them, the protection covers only those columns. To reach a chosen k, each quasi-identifier is coarsened along a hierarchy set in advance (exact age to five-year band, full postcode to district), and the values or records that would still sit in a group smaller than k are suppressed, with a search choosing the coarsening that loses least information. The output is the transformed table of real records made less specific, not artificial ones, together with the k it achieves and a measure of the detail lost. Unlike differential privacy, it gives no bound on what an observer can learn, because it blocks linking on the listed columns but does not stop someone learning a sensitive value that everyone in a group shares.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital trust preparing an extract of emergency attendances for a university research team treats age, sex, postcode district and attendance date as quasi-identifiers, since local news reports and social media posts about incidents often carry them. Using ARX it generalises age to five-year bands and dates to weeks, suppresses the records still in groups smaller than five, and sends the extract with a note of the k achieved, the columns covered and the share of records suppressed.

A national statistics office preparing a scientific-use file of a household survey for registered researchers recodes region and occupation into broader groups in sdcMicro, then applies local suppression until every combination of age band, sex, region and household size occurs at least three times, and publishes the number of suppressed values with the file so that users can judge the effect on their analyses.

A motor insurer sharing a claims table with an analytics firm that will build a fraud-detection model applies 10-anonymity to policyholder age, vehicle model and postcode district. Before release it agrees with the firm that the coarser bands still carry enough signal for the model, and it keeps the generalisation scheme so that later releases are generalised from the same scheme rather than a new one.

limitations.description: k-Anonymity hides which record is a person's, not what their group has in common. If all k records in a group share the same diagnosis, anyone who can place a person in that group learns the diagnosis, and an attacker with extra background knowledge can rule out other members of the group. Extensions such as l-diversity and t-closeness add conditions on the sensitive column for this reason; k-anonymity alone does not prevent sensitive values being disclosed.

The protection covers only the columns the data holder lists as quasi-identifiers, and rests on the holder judging correctly which columns an attacker could find elsewhere. A column left off the list, such as a rare diagnosis that a local newspaper has reported, can still single a record out, and the property says nothing about it. Choosing the list needs a realistic picture of the public, commercial and leaked data an attacker could hold.

Each release is protected only on its own. Two k-anonymous versions of the same data, generalised differently or produced at different times as records are added, can be joined to narrow groups below k, and two releases that keep the rows in the same order can be lined up row by row. Later releases must be built from the first, or treat all its released columns as quasi-identifiers, and row order must be randomised before each release.

With many quasi-identifiers or detailed values such as exact dates and measurements, most records are unique, and reaching k needs coarsening or suppression heavy enough to remove the detail an analysis or model depends on; the method suits continuous variables poorly. Because the suppressed records are those with rare combinations of values, the released table can under-represent exactly the unusual cases a model most needs to handle.

Requiring k within the released table treats the attacker as knowing their target is in it. When the table is a small sample of a larger population, a record unique in the table may match many people outside it, so the requirement over-protects; El Emam and Dankar found this over-anonymisation, and the loss of information it causes, greatest at small sampling fractions. A re-identification risk assessment against the population can justify a lighter transformation.

techniques.name: PII Detection and Redaction in Training Text
techniques.description: PII detection and redaction finds personally identifiable information (PII), such as names, email addresses, phone numbers and account or ID numbers, in a body of text and removes or replaces it before the text is used to train or fine-tune a model, so that the model has fewer personal details to memorise and later reproduce. Presidio, a widely used open-source tool first released by Microsoft and now run as an independent community project, is the reference implementation: each document passes through a set of recognisers, in which a named-entity recognition model (by default an English spaCy model) tags names, places and dates, patterns with checksum or format checks catch structured identifiers such as card and NHS numbers, and nearby words such as 'account' raise a candidate's confidence score. Every detection above a chosen score is then replaced with a placeholder for its type (for example <PERSON>), masked, hashed, encrypted or deleted, and the cleaned corpus goes to training. Because detection is never complete, the procedure ends by measuring recall, the share of identifiers actually caught, for each type on a hand-labelled sample of the same corpus. The evidence it produces is that measured miss rate and the cleaned corpus; unlike differential privacy or synthetic data, it removes real personal details from real text and gives no bound on what remains.

example_use_cases.description: A bank preparing two years of customer-service chat transcripts to fine-tune an assistant runs Presidio with added pattern recognisers for sort codes and its own account-number format, replaces each detection with a type placeholder, and has staff label 500 transcripts by hand to measure recall per entity type. It fine-tunes only once recall for names and account numbers meets the target in its data protection impact assessment, where it records the miss rate.

An NHS trust preparing discharge letters to fine-tune a summarisation model finds on a labelled sample that the default English model misses many names written in clinical shorthand and does not detect ward and bed codes at all. It adds lists of staff names and patterns for local codes, re-measures recall on a fresh labelled sample, and reports the remaining miss rate to its information governance group, which decides whether further controls are needed.

A company building a code-completion model from its internal repositories detects email addresses, IP addresses, keys and passwords with patterns and a trained detector, discards detections that are too short or are private network addresses to cut false alarms, replaces the rest with tokens such as <EMAIL> and <KEY>, and reports precision and recall per type on an annotated set of files kept apart from tuning.

limitations.description: Detection always misses some identifiers, and a model can memorise and reproduce what is missed, especially details repeated across many documents. A study that fine-tuned GPT-2 on court judgments and emails scrubbed with Presidio's default tagger and a second recogniser concluded that scrubbing reduces but cannot fully prevent leakage of personal information; Presidio's README gives no guarantee of finding it all. The evidence is a measured miss rate, not proof that none remains.

It finds only the categories it has recognisers for. On a 2022 benchmark of European Court of Human Rights judgments, Presidio's default setup caught about 70 per cent of identifying mentions but only about 45 per cent of direct identifiers, because it did not recognise case numbers, which identify the applicant on their own. Details that identify someone only in combination, such as a job title, employer and town, are not entity types at all, so redacted text can still point to a person.

The default recognisers are built for general English text. Clinical shorthand, other languages, source code and in-house identifier formats need extra recognisers or a different model, and recall measured on one corpus does not carry over to another, so the labelled sample used for the measurement must come from the corpus being cleaned and be kept apart from any tuning of the recognisers.

Raising recall by lowering the score threshold or switching on broad entity types also removes text that is not personal, such as names of public bodies, laws and places the task depends on, which lowers the value of the data for training. On the court-judgment benchmark, switching on organisation names raised Presidio's recall slightly but cut its precision from about 0.76 to 0.54.

Redaction removes identifiers from the text but does not hide whether a document was used for training, and it gives no formal bound. In the GPT-2 study, membership inference on the scrubbed model still reached an AUC of 0.82, where 0.5 is chance, and adding differentially private training brought it down to 0.5. Claims about membership, or a formal guarantee, need DP-SGD or another method alongside redaction.
